entries.teaser: This diagram lays out the paper's three-stage method: sample a language model's internal activations (residual stream, MLP, or attention sublayer) while it runs over a text corpus; train a sparse autoencoder with tied encoder and decoder weights and a ReLU bottleneck to reconstruct those activations as a sparse combination of learned directions; then interpret the resulting dictionary features, for instance by scoring them with an automated interpretability procedure. It is the map for the whole paper, since every later experiment probes one of these three stages.

resultsAndInterpretation.title: Dictionary features score higher on automated interpretability than baselines
resultsAndInterpretation.narrative: This experiment asks whether the learned dictionary features are individually more interpretable than directions found by neurons, PCA, ICA, and random baselines, using an automated procedure that has a language model describe a feature from its activating text and then predict its activation elsewhere. Table 1 and Figure 2 give the headline comparison, and the remaining figures and Table 2 in this group stress-test that result against dictionary size, scoring method, the MLP sublayer, and possible statistical confounds.

entries.teaser: Five dictionary features from the layer-1 residual stream, picked in the arbitrary order they appear in the dictionary, each paired with a GPT-4-written description and its autointerpretability score. It gives a concrete, worked example of what the automated interpretation pipeline outputs before the paper moves to aggregate comparisons, ranging from a fairly clean 'letter W' feature to a barely interpretable 'actions' feature.

This chart compares the mean autointerpretability score of the learned dictionary features against four baselines (ICA, PCA, random directions, and the untransformed neuron basis) across residual-stream layers 0 through 5. It is the paper's headline result: dictionary features score noticeably higher in early layers, though the gap narrows through the model and becomes comparable to ICA by the later layers shown.

This figure repeats the interpretability-by-layer comparison for seven different dictionary-size ratios, from half the model's dimension up to 32 times overcomplete. It shows that the interpretability advantage of sparse coding is not limited to large, overcomplete dictionaries but also holds for smaller ones, which just explain less of the overall activation variance.

This plot recomputes interpretability scores using only randomly sampled text fragments, dropping the top-activating fragments that make scoring easier. It addresses the worry that mixing high-activation examples with random ones inflates the scores, and finds that although absolute scores drop for every method, dictionary features still outperform the baselines, especially in early layers.

This pair of plots repeats the top-and-random and random-only interpretability comparisons for the MLP sublayer instead of the residual stream. It shows the approach transfers to the MLP with mixed success: many features are still more interpretable than neurons, but the paper notes elsewhere that MLP dictionaries also produce a large number of features that never activate.

This table reports the correlation between a feature's interpretability score and four statistical moments of its activation distribution: mean, variance, skew, and kurtosis. Skew and kurtosis show the strongest positive correlations, supporting the idea that interpretable features have heavy-tailed activations, which also explains why ICA, which maximizes non-Gaussianity, is the strongest of the baseline methods.

This chart adds fixed-K variants of ICA and PCA as further baselines, matching the number of directions active per token to the average number of active dictionary features. It checks whether the sparse coding advantage in Figure 2 is just an artifact of comparing directions active over an unequal share of activation space, and finds this accounts for only a small part of the difference.

resultsAndInterpretation.title: Dictionary features localize a causal behavior with fewer, smaller edits than PCA
resultsAndInterpretation.narrative: Using activation patching on the indirect object identification task, this experiment tests whether editing the model along dictionary-feature directions can reproduce a target behavior with fewer interventions and smaller edits than editing along PCA directions. Figure 3 gives the main result on one layer of Pythia-410M and Figure 17 repeats the same measurement across five additional layers.

entries.teaser: These two plots track KL divergence from a target output as more features are patched (left) and as edit magnitude grows (right), comparing sparse dictionary features to PCA components and to a non-sparse dictionary on layer 11 of Pythia-410M. Dictionary features reach a given KL divergence with fewer patches and smaller edits than PCA, and that advantage disappears for the non-sparse dictionary, indicating sparsity itself drives the improvement.

This figure reruns the same two KL-divergence measurements from Figure 3 across six residual-stream layers of Pythia-410M (layers 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, and 23) instead of just layer 11. It shows the causal-localization advantage of dictionary features over PCA is not specific to one layer but holds fairly consistently across the depth of the model.

resultsAndInterpretation.title: Individual features are monosemantic, predictable, and chainable into circuits
resultsAndInterpretation.narrative: This set of case studies zooms into a handful of hand-picked dictionary features to check three properties of a genuine feature: it fires on a single human-understandable input pattern, it has a sensible effect on output logits when removed, and its activation can be traced back through features in earlier layers. Figures 4, 11 through 15 build and stress-test the input and output story around an apostrophe feature, while Figure 5 assembles a multi-layer causal tree for a closing-parenthesis feature.

entries.teaser: This pair of histograms shows which tokens activate dictionary feature 556 (left) and which output tokens lose the most predicted probability when the feature is ablated (right). The feature fires almost exclusively on apostrophes, and removing it most strongly suppresses the model's prediction of a following 's', matching how apostrophes precede 's' in possessives and contractions like 'let's'.

This causal tree traces a layer-5 feature that fires on tokens inside parentheses and predicts a closing parenthesis, tracking backward through four earlier layers via ablation experiments to find which upstream features feed it. The resulting tree of interpretable upstream features, such as ones detecting acronyms or tokens right after an open parenthesis, demonstrates that circuit detection can be automated using dictionary features instead of individual neurons.

This histogram shows token activations for the default-basis residual-stream dimension that most resembles the apostrophe feature from Figure 4. Unlike that clean dictionary feature, this raw dimension only clusters around apostrophes at its highest activations and represents unrelated information at lower activations, illustrating the polysemanticity that sparse coding is meant to remove.

This pair of histograms shows the input activations and output-logit effects of a dictionary feature that fires on the word 'if' specifically in coding-like contexts. It is one of several worked examples used to show that individually interpretable, narrowly-scoped features recur across the learned dictionary, not just for the apostrophe case.

This pair of histograms documents a feature that fires on the 'Dis' prefix as part of specific word bigrams, such as 'disCLAIM', 'disclosed', and 'disordered'. It shows that some dictionary features track sub-word token patterns rather than whole semantic concepts, broadening the kinds of monosemantic structure the method can recover.

This pair of histograms shows a second apostrophe-related feature, one that activates specifically in 'I'll'-like contraction contexts rather than apostrophes generally. Alongside Figure 15, it shows the model uses several distinct apostrophe features tied to different families of contractions rather than one catch-all apostrophe feature.

This pair of histograms shows a third apostrophe-related feature, specific to 'don't'-like contraction contexts. Together with Figure 14, it reinforces that the single apostrophe feature highlighted in Figure 4 is only one member of a family of narrowly-scoped apostrophe features.

resultsAndInterpretation.title: Sparsity-accuracy tradeoffs that shaped the training setup
resultsAndInterpretation.narrative: These sweeps characterize how the autoencoders' training hyperparameters, chiefly the sparsity coefficient alpha and the dictionary-size ratio R, trade sparsity against reconstruction accuracy and against the number of features that stay active, providing the basis for the hyperparameter choices used in the main experiments.

entries.teaser: This plot sweeps the dictionary-size ratio for an MLP-layer-0 autoencoder and charts the tradeoff between the average number of active features and the proportion of unexplained reconstruction variance. The curve is smooth with no sharp knee, which the authors take as evidence there is no single obviously correct sparsity level to aim for.

This plot sweeps the sparsity coefficient alpha for autoencoders trained for different numbers of epochs, tracking how the sparsity-versus-unexplained-variance tradeoff shifts with more training. It shows how training length changes the achievable tradeoff curve, informing how long the dictionaries used elsewhere in the paper were trained.

This plot tracks what fraction of a dictionary's features remain active as the sparsity coefficient alpha increases, across layers and dictionary-size ratios, for both residual-stream and MLP autoencoders. It shows residual-stream dictionaries can be pushed to at least four times overcomplete before features start dying off, a finding that directly guided the alpha values used in the main interpretability experiments.
